lines.text: I woke on a grey afternoon in my own bed, with something very heavy across my legs.
It was Ash. Thin, scarred, snoring, with a streak of white down his neck I didn't recognise. He opened one eye, thumped his tail once, and went back to sleep.
I cried for a while. Ash let me. Then he lay on my chest until I stopped.
You slept for twenty-two days. I counted. I held your hand every day so it wouldn't get cold.
My fingers were black to the knuckle. The left hand, the one Nell had held, was healing faster than the right. Nobody could explain that.
Ilse told me the rest. We had lost four people at the gate. I made her tell me their names before anything else.
And while you slept, the north held a Moot. In your hall. Kesting, Marrick, Saltmouth, the Skeld, and every lord between here and the Senn with a roof left.
The King named you traitor, boy. So the north named you something else. Lord of the North. It was unanimous. You'd have argued, so we didn't wake you.
I wrote it down. In the margin, in case you forget.
Bram helped me down to the hall. My legs had forgotten how stairs worked. He pretended not to notice, which is how I knew I looked terrible.
The hall was full. Every lord, every elder, every captain in the north. And above them all, the lamp.
It didn't jump this time. It blazed, white as sun on snow, so bright every shadow in the hall fled backwards.
Six. The ceiling is six, Lucan. Nobody in the north is stuck at five any more.
Then I've somewhere to go.
And they knelt. Halvard first, complaining about his knees. Then Ysolde. Then Freydis, who had never knelt to anyone. Then the whole hall.
I hadn't asked for it. Not long ago I'd been a zero with six goats and a debt. But you don't get to refuse the people who choose you.
That evening, a lone Measurer rode to the gate under a white flag, carrying a small box with the Grand Measurer's seal.
Inside was my father's signet ring. And a letter.
Lord Lucan. Congratulations on your promotion. Your father has been tried for harbouring a hollow-born, and found guilty.
He will be executed in the Square of the Seven at noon on midwinter day, unless his son would like to take his place. I'm told you're good with numbers.
I looked up at the lamp, blazing over a hall of people who had just knelt to me. He was right. I am good with numbers.
Midwinter was thirty-four days away.
The Lord Who Measured Zero. End of season two. Chapter one hundred and twenty-one, coming soon.
